articles.title: Finland halts deportation of Russian family who ‘risked everything’ to oppose Ukraine invasion
articles.excerpt:
Mother and son Olga and Nikita Belov say they were facing jail and potential torture after asylum case was rejected

A Russian family who were on the brink of being deported from Finland after repeate...
articles.body_text:
Mother and son Olga and Nikita Belov say they were facing jail and potential torture after asylum case was rejected

A Russian family who were on the brink of being deported from Finland after repeatedly being denied asylum – despite the threat of arrest, imprisonment and torture for their pro-Ukrainian activism – have won a court appeal and will have their case reconsidered.

Nikita Belov and his mother, Olga Belov, fled their homeland for Finland in 2022 after attracting the attention of Russian authorities – including a military summons, threatening messages and attempts to locate them – for expressing opposition to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

They were due to be deported from Finland within weeks after the Finnish immigration service said they faced “no real risk” if they returned to Russia. In April they were temporarily detained by authorities pending deportation.

The administrative court has quashed the decision, citing new evidence, including media coverage in Finnish, Russian and internationally, and referred the case back to the immigration service for fresh consideration.

The Belovs’ case has gained political traction in neighbouring Norway. Last week politicians from Norway’s Green party tried to stage an intervention, proposing to the government that if the Belovs’ deportation went through, Norway should offer them asylum instead.

The political activist and Putin critic Bill Browder, who is the head of the Global Magnitsky Justice Campaign, has said the case is “a defining test of Europe’s commitment to protecting those who have risked everything to oppose Putin’s war”.

Nikita, 25, left his engineering job at a research institute in Moscow specialising in metallurgical technologies after finding out the work he was doing was connected to the Russian war effort.

Since their arrival in Finland, Nikita and Olga, 55, a nurse anaesthetist, have been vocal supporters of Ukraine, sending humanitarian aid, including to the Ukrainian armed forces.

Olga said the court’s decision marked the first positive news they had received in four years but that it was overshadowed by “constant uncertainty and fear of deportation”.

She added: “My health has deteriorated over these four years, and we still have to wait for a final decision. This is very stressful, and nobody knows how long it will take. This experience has already left a lasting mark on our lives, and we will have to cope with the consequences. No matter what, I’d like to thank everybody who helps us, supports us, and literally saves us from death.”

Nikita said: “Previously, when I imagined my reaction to a positive decision, I was sure it would be a very emotional moment. But actually, I felt nothing. It’s weird, but now it seems to me that I’m already mentally exhausted. We still have to wait for a final decision.”

Their lawyer, who requested not to be named for security reasons, hopes they will be granted asylum soon. “The court has overturned the negative asylum decision as the clients have provided so much new evidence on them being profiled as being at risk of persecution,” they said. “The international attention and vast media coverage on the case and whether it puts them at risk has to be assessed accurately by the Finnish immigration service.”

Browder, whose friend and lawyer Sergei Magnitsky died at the hands of Putin’s regime, said the latest decision was an “important victory for Nikita and Olga, but it should never have got this far”.

He added: “Finland is on the frontline of defending Europe against Putin’s aggression. It would be completely perverse for it to send two people who have stood publicly against that aggression straight back into Putin’s hands. I hope the Finnish authorities will now grant Nikita and Olga the protection they deserve.”

Antti Lehtinen, the director of the department for international protection at the Finnish immigration service, said he was unable to comment on individual cases, but added: “Only approximately 5% of all decisions are returned for reconsideration each year. The vast majority of these cases are due to the applicant presenting new information about their situation during the judicial proceedings.

“The asylum decisions of the Finnish immigration service therefore correspond well with national legal practice and are also in line with the average decision-making practices of EU member states.”

articles.title: ‘Duck Dynasty’ stars Jep and Jessica Robertson say ‘a lot of prayer’ led them to leave Louisiana for Texas
articles.excerpt:
Jep and Jess Robertson share their new life on a North Texas ranch on Great American Media’s new reality series "Jep & Jess: Beyond the Bayou."

Jep and Jessica Robertson said they did a lot of prayin...
articles.body_text:
Jep and Jess Robertson share their new life on a North Texas ranch on Great American Media’s new reality series "Jep & Jess: Beyond the Bayou."

Jep and Jessica Robertson said they did a lot of praying before they made the decision to move their family from their roots in Louisiana for a new life in North Texas.

"It was a lot of prayer, a lot to talking to our friends, but, you know, we love it out here," Jep Robertson told Fox News Digital.

The couple will share their journey on their new Great American Media series "Jep & Jess: Beyond the Bayou," which will stream exclusively on Great American Pure Flix every Thursday starting Aug. 13. It will also be available on Great American Family and GFAM+ starting Saturday, Aug. 15 at 9 p.m.

‘SOPRANOS’ STAR JAMIE-LYNN SIGLER FLED HOLLYWOOD FOR TEXAS WHERE SHE NO LONGER FEELS ‘WATCHED’

The couple will share their journey on their new Great American Media series "Jep & Jess: Beyond the Bayou," which will stream exclusively on Great American Pure Flix every Thursdays starting Aug. 13. (Aime Casillas)

"And actually, in this part of Texas where the ranch is, when I was a kid, I used to come out here with my dad from about 12 years old to about 16, 17, Jep explained. "Actually, my first kind of decent buck was killed in Texas not far from this ranch we’re filming the show on, and so I love this area of Texas."

He said it felt like "God is just like ‘All right, guys, you know, you should try this,’ and we're like ‘OK, we'll try.'"

The show follows the couple as they leave "behind the Louisiana bayous that first made them household names," to build a "new life in Texas, transforming Comanche Moon Ranch into a thriving community rooted in craftsmanship, hospitality, and legacy," according to the description of the show on Great American Family’s website. "Along the way, viewers will witness the joys and challenges of creating a place where neighbors become family, love grows deeper, and every project serves a greater purpose."

WATCH HERE: ‘DUCK DYNASTY’ STARS ON BIG MOVE AWAY FROM LOUISIANA: ‘WE LOVE IT OUT HERE’

Jep noted that it has been a few years since they had been on TV, "So our family has definitely gotten a lot bigger."

COUNTRY STAR TYLER HUBBARD SAYS ‘THE CHOSEN’ BROUGHT THE BIBLE TO LIFE FOR HIS FAMILY

"Beyond the Bayou" will also give fans a more "in-depth" look at them, Jep said, adding that it will be "faith-forward."

The first episodes, he said, show them talking to their Bible study group about "coming out here and kind of doing this whole project, and which was really cool because what most people don't know is like we didn't tell them. We were just meeting with our Bible group, and then, you know, we talked about kind of what was going on, so it's very authentic, which I thought was really cool."

Jep and Jessica Robertson have left Louisiana for Texas. (WireImage)

Jep and Jess, who are now grandparents, have been married for nearly 25 years. And while they have a strong marriage, they admit it wasn’t always easy.

"I always say, the first seven, eight years were really tough being married," Jep admitted. "I was just like, man, I can't do this.

WATCH HERE: ‘DUCK DYNASTY’ STAR JEP ROBERTSON SAYS NEW REALITY SERIES WILL GIVE ‘IN-DEPTH’ ‘FAITH-FORWARD’ LOOK AT THEIR LIVES

JESSIE JAMES DECKER ON WHY HER MARRIAGE TO ERIC DECKER HASN'T LOST ITS SPARK AFTER FOUR KIDS

The couple, however, had "so many amazing people in our lives," he said, adding that his oldest brother Alan and his wife really helped them navigate their early years as a couple.

"And so, I think it's a testament to God and the people he's put in our life, you know, just not giving up," he confessed. "When people ask me about marriage advice --- it'll be 25 years in October --- and I'm like, ‘Man, I would just say, don't give up.’ I mean, that's the main thing is don't give up."

It took them years, he said, but eventually they got on the "same team."

"It's OK if you make a mistake. It's like, ‘Oh, I screwed up here and you just forget and move on," he said. But it takes time and wisdom to learn these things."

LORENZO LAMAS FINDS HAPPINESS WITH HEATHER LOCKLEAR AFTER YEARS OF 'TRIAL AND ERROR'

Jep and Jess Robertson said they prayed a lot before they decided to move to Texas. (GC Images)

Jess added that "so many people say the first year of marriage is hard, but I always say the first seven because we were super young."

The pair met in February, started dating in June and were married by October, "so, we really got to know each other once we were married. And I say the only reason why we're still married is because we love the Lord more than we love, you know, each other. And I think when you're always pointing to him, all the things, all the hurts, all the disappointments, any little, you know comparing you to him, my father and you to my mom, all those things, it makes it OK because you're not looking for that anymore."

WATCH HERE: ‘DUCK DYNASTY' STAR JESS ROBERTSON SAYS SHE AND JEP ARE STILL TOGETHER BECAUSE THEY LOVE GOD MORE THAN EACH OTHER

She added, "And I think once, like he said, we got on the same team, we knew each other, we were on the team, I know he loves the Lord, I know he has a good heart, and so all the little things that happen, I can let it go, right?"

And as they build the ranch, where the public can visit, Jess said she thinks people are looking for a simpler, more community-oriented life.

Jess and Jep Roberston with Korie Robertson and Willie Robertson in 2013. (Getty Images for ACM)

'MASTERCHEF' FINALIST SAYS BUSY FAMILIES ARE LOSING SOMETHING MORE IMPORTANT THAN HOME-COOKED MEALS

"I've noticed like more girls, younger girls wanting to sew and learn to sew and being very creative, learning how to, you know, raise chickens and can tomatoes and make jams," she said, adding that it was encouraging to her to see younger women wanting to learn skills that meant a lot to her growing up that she learned from her grandparents.

Jess and Jep Robertson with their family (Aime Casillas)

"So, I think that that's definitely what people want," she continued. "And even if you don't have that," "Beyond the Bayou" is "a show they can watch, and it's actually some place you can actually come and experience. You don't have to actually own it, and you know live this daily. You can actually get away and have this reconnect with your family, with your friend group, family reunions."

Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Storm Lala damages bridges and more than 100 homes on Hawaii’s Big Island
articles.excerpt:
Lala was downgraded from hurricane to tropical storm Sunday, but could become a hurricane again by Wednesday

Cleanup efforts started on Hawaii after Hurricane Lala rolled past the Big Island and dump...
articles.body_text:
Lala was downgraded from hurricane to tropical storm Sunday, but could become a hurricane again by Wednesday

Cleanup efforts started on Hawaii after Hurricane Lala rolled past the Big Island and dumped heavy rain across the US Pacific state.

Lala was downgraded to a tropical storm by the time it grazed the islands, but it brought heavy rains and winds strong enough to sweep about 100 homes off their foundations on the Big Island.

Josh Green, Hawaii’s governor, said officials were still investigating whether there had been any storm-related deaths.

“We’re praying that there are essentially no fatalities. The question is a difficult one to answer in some ways,” Green said.

Randy Collins, Hawaii’s emergency management director, also warned that there were still dangers to face even though the storm had passed.

“Many casualties often happen after the disaster,” Collins told reporters. “As people are cleaning things up, they’re working with heavy equipment, chainsaws, generators. They’re working around downed power lines and so forth. That’s when the casualties come.”

Green, the Hawaii governor, estimated the storm caused hundreds of millions of dollars in damage statewide, with more than 100 homes and several bridges damaged on the Big Island.

Parts of a major highway in the Big Island’s south-east collapsed overnight, the New York Times reported, blocking road access to the town of Pahala that has the region’s only hospital.

“It’s complete and utter devastation,” Jeanne Kapela told Honolulu Civil Beat. “Families have lost their homes; the entire community is impacted,” the US representative said.

On the island of Oahu, the Honolulu fire department had received more than 600 weather-related responses by noon local time Sunday, including 147 reports of downed trees. There were also roofs blown off, downed power lines and one swimmer who had to be rescued, a city statement said.

Lala was downgraded from a hurricane to a tropical storm in the early hours of Sunday, but the National Hurricane Center warned that it could become a hurricane again by Wednesday.

Hawaii was last hit by a “major” hurricane – meaning category 3, 4, or 5 on the Saffir-Simpson scale – in 1992, when Hurricane Iniki caused at least six deaths and billions of dollars in damage.

The islands were menaced by Hurricane Fausto last month, before the storm weakened and skirted north of the island chain.

Lala comes as a powerful El Niño has formed in the central equatorial Pacific Ocean.

Temperatures are already so high that the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration predicts a 69% chance of a “historic event that would exceed the strength of previous El Niño events dating back to 1950” when it peaks between October and December.

El Niño, a natural climate pattern when sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean become unusually warm, tends to promote hurricane activity in the Pacific while suppressing it in the Atlantic.

The human-caused climate crisis can amplify El Niño’s impacts because a warmer ocean and atmosphere increase the availability of energy and moisture for extreme weather events, such as heatwaves and heavy rainfall.

articles.title: UK government ‘irresponsible’ for not publishing emergency drought plans
articles.excerpt:
Campaigners demand greater transparency into water companies’ plans not made public due to ‘security reasons’

The UK government has been accused of a lack of transparency and of acting irresponsibly ...
articles.body_text:
Campaigners demand greater transparency into water companies’ plans not made public due to ‘security reasons’

The UK government has been accused of a lack of transparency and of acting irresponsibly for refusing to publish the emergency drought plans that are produced by water companies.

Water firms are required to publish statutory drought plans every five years to detail the actions needed to ensure public water supply is maintained and the environment is protected during drought.

Water levels at five key reservoirs in England and Wales are now “exceptionally low” and three-quarters of England and the whole of Wales are in drought.

The 2027-32 drought plans, which are under consultation, detail what will happen in different scenarios, with the most extreme actions ranging from standpipes in the street to rota cuts, where water is limited to a few hours each day.

Alongside these publicly available plans, water companies are required to produce separate emergency drought plans.

A water industry source said these plans were not published to avoid alarming the public. The government said the plans were not published for security reasons.

Alastair Chisholm, the water, policy, regulation and governance lead at the consultancy firm Arup, said that in the “new normal” of the climate crisis causing droughts to become more frequent and more extreme, there would probably be situations where “some quite difficult decisions need to be taken with some quite significant imposition’s on people’s lifestyles”.

He pointed to Day Zero in Cape Town, South Africa, in 2018, when millions of households faced drastic water shortages after the worst drought to hit the city in almost a century.

“People do genuinely start to be scared that they’re not going to be able to get water to drink, and that has got all manner of sort of social connotations which is going to need to be very carefully managed,” Chisholm said.

Prof Liz Bentley, the chief executive of the Royal Meteorological Society, said it made sense not to publish these plans because drought could lead to widespread impacts on certain critical industries. For example, recent drought and extreme heat in Europe forced several nuclear power plants to shut down.

“If you start to see significant shortages of water that impact major industries then these are the kind of things you want to keep confidential because that could have widespread effects on the security of the country,” Bentley said.

In some areas of England, the impact of water shortages is already being felt. Sussex, Cambridgeshire, Suffolk and Norfolk have all seen housing and business development delayed due to water supply availability and ageing or inadequate water infrastructure.

Water shortages are also affecting food security, with global food prices at a three-year high as heatwaves, drought and war push up the cost of crops.

With water increasingly becoming a scarce commodity and as demand for water increases due to the rapid growth of water-hungry industries such as datacentres, the trade body Water UK recently told the Guardian it had asked the government to publish a drought hierarchy to set out which sectors would be prioritised in times of water shortages, but that ministers had yet to do so.

“Without this there will be a trade-off across society,” said Jon Chappell, Water UK’s deputy director.

Ollie Hayes, the head of big tech and campaigns at the campaign group Global Action Plan, said that amid increasing concern that datacentres could be prioritised over other sectors for water, it was irresponsible for the government to keep its emergency drought plans from the public.

“People are deeply anxious about dwindling water supplies and want to know what the plan is. Will water-hungry AI datacentres be prioritised in a drought emergency? The secrecy only adds to a sense that controversial decisions like this may have already been made,” he said.

The Green party leader, Zack Polanski, said it was “deeply worrying that emergency drought plans are being hidden from the public”. “People deserve to know what plans – if any – are in place to protect our water supply,” he said.

Polanski said full nationalisation of water companies must be at the top of the government’s agenda to “prevent catastrophic water shortages in the years ahead”.

On Sunday it was reported that the industry regulator, Ofwat, was considering allowing water companies to raise bills during periods of drought.

Amy Fairman, the head of campaigns at campaign group River Action, criticised the government’s overall lack of transparency over how the country will deal with drought as the climate crisis intensifies.

“My key concern is around the lack of a holistic plan to deal with water shortages going forward. There is no more precious resource than water, and yet there isn’t a national water security plan in place,” she said.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said emergency drought plans were in addition to publicly available statutory drought plans and would not be published for security reasons.

A Water UK spokesperson said: “Each water company publishes a drought plan, which is consulted on publicly and sets out the actions the company will take at each stage of a drought. Planning for a severe drought sits under a separate framework, and publication is a matter for government. We support calls from the House of Lords environment and climate change committee for the government to decide how water should be prioritised in a severe drought.”

articles.title: Trump hails Mecca pact: Can it replace the region’s US security umbrella?
articles.excerpt: Islamabad, Pakistan — When Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan signed a mutual defence pact in Mecca 10 days ago, some geopolitical analysts saw the deal as a message to Washington — that several of th...
articles.body_text:
Islamabad, Pakistan — When Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan signed a mutual defence pact in Mecca 10 days ago, some geopolitical analysts saw the deal as a message to Washington — that several of the United States’ closest military allies and partners no longer trusted its security umbrella.

On Sunday, US President Donald Trump made it clear that he didn’t mind the Middle East finding ways to defend itself.

“Very happy to see that Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan have recently, and finally, signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “It shows that the Middle East is coming together and how Countries will finally be able to defend themselves in a more meaningful way.”

Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif thanked Trump within hours on Monday, crediting his “courageous and decisive leadership” with helping avert “a nuclear catastrophe in South Asia”.

In many ways, Trump’s apparent happiness over US partners seeking other security arrangements beyond their traditional reliance on Washington is in keeping with his political posture: The US president has long accused allies of not spending enough on their own defence, and of stretching America’s resources in their service.

But even as three close US allies build their own collective defence arrangement, one question hovers as an elephant in the room, say analysts: Can deals like the Mecca pact actually replace the reliance of countries like Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia on the US?

The timing of Trump’s statement is not incidental, say analysts. The US president has spent much of the past year pushing allies to shoulder more of their own defence burden.

At NATO’s summit in The Hague in June 2025, member states agreed to more than double their defence spending target, from 2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) to 5 percent by 2035, after sustained pressure from Trump, who had questioned whether Washington should keep defending allies that fell short.

On Sunday, before his post on the Mecca pact, Trump also announced he was “substantially” reducing joint military exercises with South Korea, citing cost and his “very good relationship” with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un, while criticising Seoul for not helping the US against Iran.

Betul Dogan-Akkas, assistant professor of international relations at Ankara University, argued that Turkiye’s role in the Mecca pact should be read against that broader backdrop.

“It is obvious that the Arab Gulf states lost their deterrence since February 28, and they have to re-establish their deterrence without relying on the US,” she told Al Jazeera, referring to the date when the US and Israel launched their war on Iran, without consulting the US’s Gulf allies — who faced Iranian retaliation. “Erdogan signals to the world and to the Gulf that he can support a regional security complex, as the world’s hegemony is not doing its job properly.”

But not all analysts see Trump’s reaction as signalling a retreat from the region.

“I don’t think the US is stepping back as such, but perhaps the limits of its military presence and its impact, as well as the associated liabilities, have been exposed quite significantly, compelling all regional actors to speed up their attempts to diversify their security linkages,” said Umer Karim, an associate fellow at the Riyadh-based King Faisal Center for Islamic Research and Studies, who specialises in Gulf and Pakistani affairs.

“The US will remain in the region, but perhaps in a manner where local partners increase their own contribution and align more closely to fill the gaps left by their near-total dependence on the US,” Karim added.

Mansoor Ahmed, an honorary lecturer at the Australian National University’s Strategic and Defence Studies Centre, took a different view.

“The Trump administration is following a graduated retrenchment as it seeks to rebuild the US military-industrial base, and is asking allies and partners to take greater responsibility for their own defence,” he told Al Jazeera.

Even so, Ahmed does not see the pact itself as a product of that retrenchment.

“While the Mecca pact inadvertently and indirectly helps US retrenchment, it was conceived and planned independently of any shifts in US policy or posture,” he said.

“It was a response to the loss of credibility of US will and capability to effectively defend the GCC countries during the US-Iran conflict,” Ahmed added, referring to the Gulf Cooperation Council countries: Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain.

For Ankara, Dogan-Akkas said, the calculation is about status as much as security.

“The main strategic gain for Turkiye is not to support its national security; its primary gain is to underline its role as a security provider, rather than a security consumer,” she said.

Gokhan Ereli, an international relations expert and assistant professor at Istanbul’s Ibn Haldun University, sees Turkiye’s willingness to bind itself to two non-NATO partners in similar terms, but traces it to Ankara’s long-standing doubts about Washington.

“Where the Gulf states fear that the American umbrella has holes, Ankara suspects the umbrella was never really held over it in the first place,” he told Al Jazeera.

He called the pact “a hedge with Turkish characteristics”, adding that the posture is “not anti-American so much as post-dependent”.

The Mecca agreement states that an armed attack on one member “shall be regarded as an attack against them all”, language modelled on NATO’s Article 5.

But Turkiye’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said a state under attack would first have to request assistance and specify what kind of help it wants — whether intelligence, logistics or troops.

Ahmed sees similar discretion built into the pact itself.

“Each country is likely to be sovereign in determining the timing, nature, extent and scope of the military assistance from the other two parties, or if any assistance is required in the first place,” he said.

Reza Khanzadeh, a Middle East analyst at George Mason University, points to precedent suggesting the clause is unlikely to drag its signatories automatically into each other’s wars.

The bilateral Saudi-Pakistan pact signed in September 2025 “did not result in a wider conflict” after Iran and then the Houthis attacked Saudi Arabia this year, he said.

Karim agrees that the commitments are conditional rather than fixed.

“This is an alignment that provides additional defence options and resources to every country but doesn’t really replace existing capabilities,” he said.

The practicality of those commitments, he explained, depends on the needs of the country under attack, with a hierarchy developing “in accordance with the needs, resources, platform availability and nature of the threat” that determines what each side can actually spare.

Still, Karim calls it a genuine institutional first, “a new thing in the region since the time of the Baghdad Pact or CENTO”.

The Baghdad Pact, renamed the Central Treaty Organization (CENTO) in 1959, was a Cold War-era alliance linking Turkiye, Iran, Pakistan, Iraq and the United Kingdom against Soviet expansion, with Washington backing it but never becoming a full member. It collapsed in 1979 after the Iranian revolution.

That ambiguity cuts both ways. It allows Riyadh, Ankara and Islamabad to project unity without directly provoking Iran.

But it also means the pact, for now, is nowhere near matching the roughly 50,000 US troops stationed across the region.

Karim is cautious about how far that gap can close.

“It all depends on the security needs of the three states, how extensive their trilateral alignment is, and the nature of the threat they are facing,” he said.

“In any case, this does create a workable alternative, but considering the structural reliance of Gulf states on the US, it doesn’t really replace it. It should be considered as adding a separate layer of deterrence.”

articles.title: French Serie A footballer Yael Trepy in intensive care after near-drowning
articles.excerpt:
French footballer Yael Trepy, who plays for Serie A club Cagliari, is in intensive care, the Italian club has confirmed, with media reporting that the 20-year-old nearly drowned in a swimming pool.

C...
articles.body_text:
French footballer Yael Trepy, who plays for Serie A club Cagliari, is in intensive care, the Italian club has confirmed, with media reporting that the 20-year-old nearly drowned in a swimming pool.

Cagliari said that Trepy “is currently in intensive care at the hospital in Sassari,” adding that the club remains “in close contact with the medical staff and the player’s family”.

“The club asks for privacy to be respected and will provide further updates as soon as possible,” Cagliari said in a statement, without disclosing the circumstances of the incident.

Italian media reported that Trepy had to be rescued on Sunday after swallowing a lot of water in a swimming pool in Porto Cervo, northern Sardinia.

Doctors placed him in a medically induced coma, the reports added.

Trepy, a forward who scored once in eight Serie A appearances last season, joined Cagliari’s academy in 2022 from Paris-based team Union Sportive Creteil.

Cagliari were last in action on Friday, beating Arezzo 1-0 in the Coppa Italia, with Trepy playing for 54 minutes.

articles.title: Donald Trump threatens to bomb Oman if it ‘gets in the way’ of ending Iran war
articles.excerpt:
President issues threat to ‘bomb the shit out of them’ after previously threatening Gulf ally in May

Donald Trump has again threatened to bomb Oman if it “gets in the way” of his effort to end the US...
articles.body_text:
President issues threat to ‘bomb the shit out of them’ after previously threatening Gulf ally in May

Donald Trump has again threatened to bomb Oman if it “gets in the way” of his effort to end the US-Israel war on Iran.

“If Oman gets in the way, we’ll bomb the shit out of them,” Trump told Fox News on Monday, the second time he has directed such a threat at Muscat, a longtime US strategic partner that has traditionally served as a key backchannel between Washington and Tehran.

The US president delivered the threat as he struggles to draw the conflict to a conclusion, almost six months after it was launched, and as a diplomatic window agreed with Tehran ran out with no final agreement in sight. But Trump also claimed during Monday’s interview that he is “not in a hurry” to reach a deal.

That two-month window for a negotiated settlement closed on Monday without a breakthrough. Trump has repeatedly claimed the war would end “soon”, and talked up the prospect of a lasting peace deal in recent months, without such a breakthrough materializing.

In the same interview, Trump said Iran should “put up the white flag of surrender”, but signaled he was not about to impose a fresh deadline on Tehran. “I have no time schedule. I’m not in a hurry,” he said.

Trump signed a memorandum of understanding with Iran at the Palace of Versailles on 17 June, on the sidelines of the G7 summit, which had paused hostilities and set a maximum 60-day window – extendable only by mutual consent – for the two sides to reach a comprehensive deal covering sanctions relief, Iran’s nuclear program and other disputes.

Trump also dismissed concerns that Washington’s own arsenal was being depleted by nearly six months of fighting, telling Fox News that what the US had expended against Iran so far is “peanuts”.

He suggested many of the US’s more advanced munitions, including air defense systems, had already been “given away” to Ukraine under his predecessor, Joe Biden – a claim that echoes warnings from defense analysts earlier in the war that US and allied stockpiles were being drawn down faster than they could be replenished.

The remarks came after Trump used his Truth Social platform to restate his negotiating red line. “The number one Goal is, and always will be, that Iran cannot have, in any way, shape, or form, a Nuclear Weapon,” he wrote.

The strait of Hormuz – a crucial chokepoint for global trade, through which about a fifth of the world’s seaborne oil supplies typically pass – has been all but closed since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in February.

Iran is to the north of the strait. Oman is to the south. The two countries have been in talks over control of the strait.

In a casual aside at a cabinet meeting in May, the president also threatened to “blow up”  Oman if it failed to “behave”.

It comes after Trump also threatened to declare the strait of Hormuz as “a territory of the United States” during a speech on Friday.

In addition to Oman’s decades-long military and economic ties with the US, the Gulf nation of 5.3 million people has played a mediation role in the war and has itself come under attack from Tehran.

Iran’s foreign ministry said on Monday that talks with Oman were “continuing in earnest”, despite Trump’s latest outburst.

Trump also confirmed for the first time that Washington had opened a direct backchannel to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which the US and Israel have targeted throughout the conflict.

“They’re good poker players, but they’re dying,” he said of the IRGC leadership.

articles.title: Charlie Kirk’s murder sends shockwaves through Christian academy in hit Fox Nation series
articles.excerpt:
